basis: New mission, no workbook source. Researched via WebSearch (Sep 2026). Key facts: Taiwan relative poverty rate ~6.75-7.53% 2017-2023, 7.43% in 2022 (MOHW); low-income children (0-18) fell 117,012 (2016) to 90,245 (2021), near-poor children fell 135,819 (2016) to 107,010 (2021), together ~200,000 in 2021 (MOHW/CRC 兒少統計專區); Child Welfare League Foundation (兒福聯盟) survey: 20% of disadvantaged children have gone hungry at home and eaten snacks instead of a meal; ~20% rely on snacks when school lunch stops over long holidays; 11.0% of students skip breakfast 3+ days/week and arrive hungry; school lunch policy expanding city by city: Taipei free for all public+private elem/JHS since Sept 2025 (NT$87/NT$92 per meal); Kaohsiung free from 2026 school year (~NT$1.8B/yr, ~180,000 students); Tainan (~NT$56/meal) and Chiayi County (~NT$62/meal) free from 2026; Pingtung County free from 2026; Hsinchu City partial subsidy (NT$40/NT$45) with full waiver for disadvantaged (city government press releases, CNA, 風傳媒, 造咖); 2026 revision of 財政收支劃分法 ended central subsidy for domestic school-lunch ingredients, shifting cost to local budgets; Alliance of Taiwan Foodbanks (台灣食物銀行聯合會, ATF) — ~60 member food banks, ~300 partner NPOs, ~100 community refrigerators (84 fridges+16 freezers) nationwide, Taipei flagship store rescues ~20,000 kg food/yr for 200+ households/month, Hualien warehouse stores 500+ tonnes serving 20+ remote communities/schools (atf.tw); retail food waste — supermarkets/hypermarkets declared ~69,670 tonnes discarded Mar 2017-Jun 2023 (6 yrs), ~11,000 tonnes/yr, ~30 tonnes/day (foodnext.net/食力, government-mandated reporting). Level is carried by syntax and lexical load per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, not by word count.

slides.1: Visibly hungry classmates rarely cross paths with most university students here, and that absence really raises an uncomfortable question worth confronting directly. Would you actually recognise one if you did?
slides.2: Specialists use the term hidden hunger for something different from having zero food available at all. It simply means food arriving unpredictably, or never in a properly sufficient amount for anyone.
slides.3: Corner stores saturate nearly every single city block in Taiwan. Despite that, almost 200,000 Taiwanese children were still officially classified as poor or near-poor in the most recent count.
slides.4: A nationwide study found that approximately one-fifth of children in low-income households have gone without an adequate meal at home. Many simply relied on snack food as a substitute instead.
slides.5: School lunch, for a considerable share of these children, effectively works out as the single meal they can always count on. That reliable anchor point disappears the moment summer begins.
slides.6: One in nine students reportedly skips breakfast more than half the school week, sitting through lessons while genuinely hungry. Hidden hunger consequently resembles fatigue in class, rather than visible starvation.
slides.7: Genuine momentum has started building recently. Since September 2025, Taipei has provided free lunch to every public and private pupil, covering both elementary and junior high school this year for good.
slides.8: A wider rollout is already underway elsewhere too. Kaohsiung's contribution alone runs to roughly 1.8 billion dollars yearly, reaching an estimated 180,000 pupils when the scheme takes full effect.
slides.9: Food banks are likewise stepping in to close whatever gaps persist. The Alliance currently runs around 100 shared fridges across the island, connecting 60 separate food banks with almost 300 partner charities.
slides.10: No single national formula governs this. Subsidies vary municipality by municipality, from around 40 dollars a meal in some places to over 90 elsewhere, producing an uneven yet rapidly shifting picture.
slides.11: Distributing canned goods is no longer the whole story for food banks. Taipei's largest operation salvages close to 20,000 kilograms annually, sustaining more than 200 households on a monthly basis.
slides.12: Should a community lack that established trust and delivery system, however, perfectly good food ends up discarded rather than reaching anyone in need. Converting near-expired bread into an actual meal demands genuine effort.
slides.13: Few people openly acknowledge this particular catch, unfortunately. Genuine access to free lunch still depends entirely on the specific school where a child happens to be enrolled during that year.
slides.14: In 2026, a funding law altered this whole picture quite a bit. Central government subsidy for all locally sourced ingredients was cancelled, meaning each municipality must now absorb that expense independently.
slides.15: The flip side involves considerable waste, however. Roughly 11,000 tonnes get discarded annually by large retailers alone, even as food banks continue struggling to reach every family requiring help.
slides.16: Taiwan genuinely possesses sufficient food today, and increasingly sufficient policy as well. What remains absent is one consistent, equitable system, rather than one that depends on luck or postcode alone.
slides.17: In summary, hidden hunger here was never fundamentally about a genuine national food shortage. It concerns food that fails to reliably reach every child, on every single day of the year.
slides.18: This gap needs genuine engineering solutions, things like smart routing software and much better delivery infrastructure. Which could easily describe someone studying exactly what you are pursuing right here and now.
slides.19: Next time you happen to notice a community fridge, or a donation bin for a food bank, consider something worth remembering. It is quietly filling a gap that policy has not yet closed.
slides.20: Adequate stock at a food bank ought never genuinely hinge on random chance. The genuine objective is engineering a dependable system where every child receives a proper meal, day in and day out.
